name: Pochvennichestvo
summary: Pochvennichestvo, 'native soil' thought, was the programme of the Dostoevsky brothers' journals Vremya and Epokha in the early 1860s. It held that Peter's reforms had split the educated estate from the common people and that Russia should reconcile the two by returning the educated to the people's native soil, building its own forms of life while keeping European learning, without the enmity of estates seen in Europe, and it put mass literacy first.
scope: The profile covers the early-1860s programme of Vremya (1861-63) and Epokha (1864-65), set out in Dostoevsky's 1860 subscription announcement and his 1862 article Two Camps of Theorists, with Grigor'ev and Strakhov as the other editors, as Hudspith and Alekseeva describe it. It excludes Dostoevsky's later nationalism and the Writer's Diary, Slavophilism, Westernism and Strakhov's later views. The defining texts are about culture, the people and education, so most economic, governmental and world statements are left null.

authors.quote: Dostoevskii was allowed to return to European Russia in 1859.
It is fair to say that Grigor'ev was the key figure in pochvennichestvo.
critics Nikolai Strakhov and Apollon Grigor'ev.

notes: Only five statements are answered: the sources are two short journal texts and two scholarly accounts, all about reconciliation of the educated with the people, native forms and education. Themes searched without finding a position: government and elections, economy and property, religion and state (Hudspith says religion was suppressed in Vremya), world affairs, war, liberty and law, technology and ecology. The shared journal programme is kept apart from Dostoevsky's later views. A check of the local corpora for Dostoevsky, Strakhov and Grigor'ev found no further defining text.
